steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on learning agile bipedal motions on a quadrupedal robot. Motivate why a quadruped is worth using for human-like motions, explain the control and motion-representation challenges, describe our hierarchical framework, and summarize what we demonstrate on the real robot.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation: human-like motions; bipeds vs. quadrupeds
2. Challenge 1: standing up and balancing on two feet
3. Challenge 2: representing a wide range of human-like motions
4. Our hierarchical framework
5. Real-robot demonstrations

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
- versatile human-like motions -> robots coexist/interact better with humans
- bipedal robots: structural similarity to humans, potential to mimic human behaviors
- but existing bipeds expensive, heavy, power-consuming
- quadrupeds: cheaper, lightweight, impressive sporting capabilities in various domains
- question: can quadrupeds do agile human-like motions as affordable alternative to humanoids?

2. Stand-up and balance
- quadrupeds designed for dog-like behavior, four legs on ground
- must stand upright on two feet from four-leg rest pose first
- stand-up needs agile policy: enough momentum to swing up, avoid flipping over
- bipedal motions inherently unstable with spherical feet -> adjust all body parts to balance
- previous work: external mechanical support; ours: no external hardware

3. Motion representation
- kinematics/dynamics differ between humans and quadrupeds
- hard to directly track human motion capture data and stay balanced
- encodings must represent versatile behaviors and be feasible for quadruped embodiment -> careful design

4. Framework
- hierarchical
- low level: motion-conditioned policy, model-free RL, balance on two toes + track reference motions
- motions = sequence of desired state of robot base + end effectors of front limbs; flexible, plausible to execute
- trained in calibrated simulator, transferred to real robot
- high level: motion generator, human-like motions from videos or natural language -> desired targets for low-level policy

5. Demonstrations
- Xiaomi CyberDog2 (\sim $1800), affordable
- boxing (Fig. 1) and ballet dance from human videos, greeting from natural language, walking hand-in-hand with a human
- first time on a quadrupedal robot

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Giving robots versatile motions like humans has been an important research topic, because it lets them coexist and interact with humans better. Bipedal robot systems have attracted a lot of interest, since their structure is similar to human beings and so they have an appealing potential to mimic human behaviors. But existing bipedal robots are usually expensive, heavy, and use a lot of power. Quadrupedal robots on the other hand are much cheaper and more lightweight, and recently they have shown impressive sporting capabilities in different domains. So an interesting question comes up: can quadrupedal robots show agile human-like motions, as an affordable alternative to humanoid robots?

Getting a quadrupedal robot to do agile bipedal motions is a hard control problem. Quadrupedal robots are designed for dog-like behaviors with four legs on the ground, so they first have to stand upright on two feet from a four-leg pose at rest before they can do the motions of bipedal creatures. To stand up, the robot needs an agile control policy that gains enough momentum to swing the robot up but at the same time does not let it flip over. Also, bipedal motions are inherently unstable on common quadrupedal robots with spherical feet, so after the robot stands up it has to actively adjust all its body parts to stay balanced. Previous work used external mechanical support to help the robot stand up. We want to control a quadrupedal robot to mimic bipedal motions without any external hardware.

Another challenge is how to master a wide range of human-like motions. Humans and quadrupedal robots differ in kinematics and dynamics, so it is difficult to directly track human motion capture data and keep the quadruped robot balanced at the same time. The motion encodings need to represent versatile human-like behaviors and also be feasible for the embodiment of a quadrupedal robot, so they have to be designed carefully.

4. Framework
- hierarchical
- low level: motion-conditioned policy, model-free RL, balance on two toes + track reference motions
- motions = sequence of desired state of robot base + end effectors of front limbs; flexible, plausible to execute
- trained in calibrated simulator, transferred to real robot
- high level: motion generator, human-like motions from videos or natural language -> desired targets for low-level policy

5. Demonstrations
- Xiaomi CyberDog2 (\sim $1800), affordable
- boxing (Fig. 1) and ballet dance from human videos, greeting from natural language, walking hand-in-hand with a human
- first time on a quadrupedal robot

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Giving robots versatile motions like humans has been an important research topic, because it lets them coexist and interact with humans better. Bipedal robot systems have attracted a lot of interest, since their structure is similar to human beings and so they have an appealing potential to mimic human behaviors. But existing bipedal robots are usually expensive, heavy, and use a lot of power. Quadrupedal robots on the other hand are much cheaper and more lightweight, and recently they have shown impressive sporting capabilities in different domains. So an interesting question comes up: can quadrupedal robots show agile human-like motions, as an affordable alternative to humanoid robots?

Getting a quadrupedal robot to do agile bipedal motions is a hard control problem. Quadrupedal robots are designed for dog-like behaviors with four legs on the ground, so they first have to stand upright on two feet from a four-leg pose at rest before they can do the motions of bipedal creatures. To stand up, the robot needs an agile control policy that gains enough momentum to swing the robot up but at the same time does not let it flip over. Also, bipedal motions are inherently unstable on common quadrupedal robots with spherical feet, so after the robot stands up it has to actively adjust all its body parts to stay balanced. Previous work used external mechanical support to help the robot stand up. We want to control a quadrupedal robot to mimic bipedal motions without any external hardware.

Another challenge is how to master a wide range of human-like motions. Humans and quadrupedal robots differ in kinematics and dynamics, so it is difficult to directly track human motion capture data and keep the quadruped robot balanced at the same time. The motion encodings need to represent versatile human-like behaviors and also be feasible for the embodiment of a quadrupedal robot, so they have to be designed carefully.

In this work we present a hierarchical framework for agile bipedal motions on a quadrupedal robot. At the low level, we use model-free reinforcement learning (RL) to train a motion-conditioned policy that can balance the quadrupedal robot on its two toes and track reference motions at the same time. Motions are represented as a sequence of the desired state of the robot base and of the end effectors of the front limbs. This representation is flexible enough to encode a spectrum of behaviors and is plausible for the quadrupedal robot to execute. We train the policy in a calibrated simulator and then transfer it to the real robot. At the high level, a motion generator takes human-like motions from videos or natural language descriptions and parameterizes them into a sequence of desired targets for the low-level policy.

We demonstrate the framework on Xiaomi CyberDog2, an affordable quadruped platform (\sim $1800). We show successful deployment of a variety of agile bipedal maneuvers and interactions with humans, for example mimicking human videos to practice boxing (Fig. 1) and ballet dance, greeting commanded by natural language instructions, and walking hand-in-hand with a human. As far as we know, this is the first time these agile bipedal motions are made possible on a quadrupedal robot.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Empowering robots with versatile motions like humans has been an important research topic, as it allows them to better coexist and interact with humans [1]. Developing bipedal robot systems has attracted much interest, since their structural similarity to human beings gives them an appealing potential to mimic human behaviors [2]. However, existing bipedal robots are typically expensive, heavy, and power-consuming [3,4,5]. In contrast, quadrupedal robots are much cheaper and more lightweight, and have recently demonstrated impressive sporting capabilities in various domains [6,7,8]. This raises an interesting question: Is it possible for quadrupedal robots to demonstrate agile human-like motions as an affordable alternative to humanoid robots?

Enabling a quadrupedal robot to perform agile bipedal motions poses significant control challenges. Since quadrupedal robots are designed for dog-like behaviors with four legs on the ground, they must first stand upright on two feet from a four-leg pose at rest to unlock the motions of bipedal creatures. The stand-up procedure requires an agile control policy that gains enough momentum to swing up the robot while avoiding flipping over. Furthermore, bipedal motions are inherently unstable on common quadrupedal robots with spherical feet, so once the robot stands up it must actively adjust all its body parts to stay balanced. Previous work used external mechanical support for the robot to stand up [9], whereas we aim to control a quadrupedal robot to mimic bipedal motions without any external hardware.

Another notable challenge is mastering a wide range of human-like motions. Due to the differences in kinematics and dynamics between humans and quadrupedal robots, it is difficult to directly track human motion capture data while keeping the quadruped robot balanced [10]. Therefore, motion encodings that both represent versatile human-like behaviors and are feasible for the embodiment of a quadrupedal robot require careful design.

In this work, we present a hierarchical framework that enables agile bipedal motions on a quadrupedal robot. At the low level, we train a motion-conditioned policy with model-free reinforcement learning (RL) that can balance the quadrupedal robot on its two toes while tracking reference motions at the same time. We represent motions as a sequence of the desired state of the robot base and end effectors of the front limbs, which is flexible enough to encode a spectrum of behaviors and plausible for the quadrupedal robot to execute. The policy is trained in a calibrated simulator and then transferred to the real robot. At the high level, a motion generator parameterizes human-like motions from videos or natural language descriptions into a sequence of desired targets for the low-level policy.

We demonstrate the whole framework on an affordable quadruped platform, Xiaomi CyberDog2 (\sim $1800) [11], and showcase the successful deployment of a variety of agile bipedal maneuvers and interactions with humans, such as mimicking human videos to practice boxing (Fig. 1) and ballet dance, greeting commanded by natural language instructions, and walking hand-in-hand with a human. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time these agile bipedal motions are made possible on a quadrupedal robot.
